items.value: Statements 1 and 2 only — heavy dependence on fossil fuels and the limited (finite) availability of resources
items.reasoning: The passage states that current production models 'rely heavily on fossil fuels' and that 'this is unsustainable because the resources are finite' — so statement 1 (fossil-fuel dependence) and statement 2 (limited availability of resources) are both named as causes. Statement 3 is the opposite of a cause: expanding recycling is listed among the steps some developed countries have taken to 'alleviate the worst effects'. With 3 excluded and 1 included, option A is the only code that fits.

items.value: Statement 1 only — by making clean energy sources available at low cost
items.reasoning: The passage says developing countries 'are hampered by the high costs and low availability of clean energy sources', so making clean energy cheap and available (statement 1) is the support the text points to. Statement 2 invents a mechanism — concessional loans for public transport — that appears nowhere; the passage mentions public transport only as something developed countries invested in for themselves. That rules out options B and D. Statement 3 (encouraging a change in production and consumption patterns) is also not offered as a form of support, which rules out C, leaving A.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 only — depletion of the soil resource and lack of water for cultivation
items.reasoning: The passage predicts that 'soil erosion by wind and water will increase', which is depletion of the soil resource (statement 1), and describes former forest tracts as 'brown earth, bare of vegetation, without any water in the streams and springs except in the rainy season', with agriculture becoming impossible — that is lack of water for cultivation (statement 3). Statement 2, a shortage of land for the common man, is never raised; the passage's worry is that existing land becomes unusable, not that land becomes scarce.

Each term is obtained by multiplying the previous term by a factor that rises by 0.5 each step: 20 x 0.5 = 10, 10 x 1 = 10, 10 x 1.5 = 15, 15 x 2 = 30, 30 x 2.5 = 75. The next multiplier is 3, so X = 75 x 3 = 225.

items.value: 8 — the middle three digits can sum to 8 (from 7412589)
items.reasoning: The seven digits 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9 sum to 36, so the whole number is divisible by 9 automatically. The 5-digit prefix must end in 5, so the 5th digit is 5; the 2nd, 4th and 6th digits must be even, so they are 2, 4 and 8 in some order. For the 6-digit prefix to be divisible by 3 the last digit must be 9. The 3-digit prefix forces the 2nd digit to be 4, and the 4th digit to be 2 (since the two-digit ending must be divisible by 4). Only 1472589 and 7412589 survive; their middle three digits are 725 (sum 14) and 125 (sum 8). Of the four choices only 8 occurs.

Take the common 50 m run as heading north to point P. X turns right (east) 60 m, then left (north) 50 m, ending 60 m east and 50 m north of P. Y turns left (west) 40 m, then right (north) 50 m, ending 40 m west and 50 m north of P. Both end on the same north line, so the separation is purely east-west: 60 + 40 = 100 m.

1 January 2000 was a Saturday. From then to 1 January 2099 is 99 years containing 25 leap days (2000, 2004, ... 2096), i.e. 99 x 365 + 25 = 36160 days; 36160 leaves remainder 5 on division by 7, so 1 January 2099 is a Thursday. 2099 is not a leap year, so 1 June is 31 + 28 + 31 + 30 + 31 = 151 days later; 151 leaves remainder 4, making 1 June 2099 a Monday. The first Sunday of that month is therefore 7 June.

items.value: All three statements are not correct
items.reasoning: With a notes of Rs 50, b of Rs 20 and c of Rs 10, a + b + c = 50 and 50a + 20b + 10c = 1840. Subtracting five times the first from the second gives 4a + b = 134, so b = 134 - 4a and c = 3a - 84; non-negativity forces a between 28 and 33. The only possible combinations are (28,22,0), (29,18,3), (30,14,6), (31,10,9), (32,6,12) and (33,2,15). None has 25 fifty-rupee notes, none has 35 twenty-rupee notes, and none has 20 ten-rupee notes, so all three statements are incorrect.

Write every number as a power of 2 where possible: 4^18 = 2^36 and 8^12 = 2^36, so those two are equal, and 2^40 is larger than both. For 3^21, note 3^21 = (3^7)^3 = 2187^3 while 2^36 = (2^12)^3 = 4096^3, so 3^21 is smaller than 2^36. Numerically 3^21 = 10,460,353,203 against 2^36 = 68,719,476,736 and 2^40 = 1,099,511,627,776. Hence 3^21 is the smallest. Note that options C and D are two different ways of writing the same number, 2^36; that does not affect the answer, since neither is the smallest.

Only four three-digit numbers n satisfy the condition that n, 2n and 3n together use each of the digits 1 to 9 exactly once: 192/384/576, 219/438/657, 273/546/819 and 327/654/981. The first row must be built from three of the digits 2, 3, 7 and 9. That excludes 192 (digits 1, 9, 2) and 219 (digits 2, 1, 9), each of which needs the digit 1. It leaves 273 and 327, so 2 combinations are possible.

items.value: We assume that in a democracy, any politician is qualified to administer a State
items.reasoning: The author's point is the incongruity he states outright: for shoe-making or medicine we insist on trained competence, yet 'in politics, we presume that everyone who knows how to get votes knows how to administer a State'. Option A is that presumption, and is the one choice contained entirely within the passage. Option D is the opposite of the author's view, since his whole purpose is to question that eligibility. Option B ('trained in administration') and option C ('devise a method of barring incompetence') both add prescriptions the passage never makes — the author asks only that we look for 'the wisest and the best'. B is the closest runner-up, and a reader who treats the closing rhetorical question as the message rather than the opening contrast could defend it.

items.value: Because it treats poverty as nothing more than meagre income or buying capacity
items.reasoning: The passage's single stated criticism of how India counts the poor is that the poverty line 'exclusively relies on the notion of poverty as insufficient income or insufficient purchasing power', which the author labels income poverty and calls only one aspect of deprivation. Option D states exactly that. Options B and C introduce rural-urban diversity and the absence of a global standard, neither of which appears in the text, and option A speaks of 'confusion' about the poverty line where the passage says only that its definition of who is poor is extremely narrow. The judgement call is that the passage lists the 'debatable methodology' and the underlying income assumption as separate grounds; D is nonetheless the only choice the passage supports.

items.value: Because it captures only one kind of deprivation and ignores all the others
items.reasoning: The passage says that 'if poverty is ultimately about deprivations affecting human well-being, then income poverty is only one aspect of it' — one deprivation among many, which is option A. Option B is contradicted by the closing lines, where low incomes and meagre possessions are said to matter precisely because they curtail capabilities, so the other deprivations are connected to purchasing power rather than unrelated to it. Options C and D introduce a time dimension the passage never raises.

items.value: All deprivations in a life, arising not only from lack of income but from the lack of real opportunities
items.reasoning: The author defines it directly: poverty of a life 'lies not merely in the impoverished state in which the person actually lives, but also in the lack of real opportunity... to choose other types of living'. Option A carries both halves of that definition. Option B keeps only the impoverished state and option C only the missed opportunities, so each is half the definition. Option D adds 'permanently', a claim the passage does not make.

Running in the same direction, the faster runner passes the slower one each time he gains a full lap of 300 m. With speeds in the ratio 3 : 2, when X has covered a distance d the gap is d - (2/3)d = d/3. The race is 3 km, so when X finishes he has run 3000 m and the gap is 1000 m, which contains 3 full laps of 300 m (gains of 300, 600 and 900 m). Hence X passes Y 3 times. The judgement call is where the race ends: if instead the slower runner were also allowed to complete 3 km, the gap would reach 1500 m and the count would be 5, which is why option D is offered; the standard reading is that the race is over when the winner finishes.

Reversing the alphabet maps each letter of position n to the letter of position 27 - n: A to Z, B to Y, and so on. Applying this letter by letter, L (12) becomes O (15), U (21) becomes F (6), C (3) becomes X (24), K (11) becomes P (16), N (14) becomes M (13), O (15) becomes L (12) and W (23) becomes D (4). LUCKNOW therefore becomes OFXPMLD. The distractors differ only in the second letter (G instead of F) or the last (E instead of D).

Every match has exactly one loser and no match is drawn, so each match eliminates precisely one player. To leave a single champion out of 150 entrants, 149 players must be eliminated, which requires 149 matches. The count does not depend on how the draw is arranged or on byes.

A number divisible by 5 ends in 0 or 5, and since every digit must be odd the units digit has to be 5. The hundreds and tens digits are then chosen without repetition from the remaining odd digits 1, 3, 7 and 9, giving 4 choices for the hundreds place and 3 for the tens place. That is 4 x 3 = 12 numbers (135, 175, 195, 315, 375, 395, 715, 735, 795, 915, 935, 975).

items.value: Neither statement alone nor both together are sufficient
items.reasoning: Statement 1 alone fails: x = 1 makes x/3 a non-integer and x an integer, while x = 0.5 makes x/3 a non-integer and x a non-integer. Statement 2 alone fails: x = 1 makes 3x an integer with x an integer, while x = 1/3 makes 3x = 1 an integer with x not an integer. Taken together they still fail, because x = 1 and x = 1/3 both satisfy both statements (for x = 1/3, x/3 = 1/9 is not an integer and 3x = 1 is) yet give opposite answers. So the question cannot be settled.

Successive percentage changes multiply. Starting from a price of 100, a 25% rise gives 125, a 20% fall gives 125 x 0.8 = 100, and a 10% rise gives 110. Equivalently 1.25 x 0.8 x 1.1 = 1.1, so the net effect is an increase of 10%.
